sysd-msg-089.title: Code sharing between microservices
sysd-msg-089.text: Ideally, microservices follow a share-nothing architecture. In practice, code must often be shared across services. Common approaches are separate shared libraries for reusable components such as a security library, replicating stable modules with minimal changes across services, or consolidating several microservices into one. Each approach has its own advantages and trade-offs, depending on context and requirements.

sysd-msg-084.title: Microservice granularity: how small is small enough
sysd-msg-084.text:
How big should a service be? The right granularity is found through iterative collaboration between architects and developers, and it is ultimately set by business drivers. Neal Ford's integrator factors, such as shared transactions or tightly coupled processes, favor combining services. His disintegrator factors, such as surviving faults or independent scalability, favor splitting them.

Very fine-grained services are easier to test and deploy independently. They tend to have lower performance and reliability, because of more communication between services and more complex choreography. Coarse-grained services are more robust and reliable, thanks to less communication overhead, but harder to test and deploy, because a change affects a wider scope.

sysd-msg-088.title: Reach-in reporting antipattern
sysd-msg-088.text:
A reporting service needs data that lives inside other services, and pulling it out directly causes trouble. Retrieving the data can break the bounded contexts of microservices, reduce the timeliness of the data, or both. This holds whether the data is pulled directly from databases, retrieved via HTTP or collected in batches. The pattern is called the reach-in reporting antipattern.

The alternative is for the databases to push the needed data to the reporting service asynchronously. Pushing needs a separate contract between the microservices and the reporting service, and it can be complex. But it preserves bounded contexts while keeping data timely.

sysd-msg-090.title: Testing and observing microservices
sysd-msg-090.text: Many independently deployed services must stay testable and visible. Sam Newman suggests keeping microservice interfaces stable and making backward-compatible changes as they evolve, so deployments need not be coordinated across services. He proposes consumer-driven contract testing as a better alternative to traditional end-to-end testing. To keep the system visible, he suggests log aggregation, metrics aggregation and {{ref:sysd-msg-145}}. Richards and Ford propose that each microservice have its own architectural characteristics, rather than uniform ones for the whole distributed system.

sysd-msg-144.title: Consul: from service discovery to service networking
sysd-msg-144.text: Consul is a service networking platform developed by HashiCorp, and it was first released as a service discovery platform. Registered services and nodes can be queried through either a DNS interface or an HTTP interface. It also provides a service mesh for secure service segmentation across any cloud or runtime, and distributed key-value storage for application configuration. The Envoy proxy provides security, visibility and resilience for all application traffic. Consul can also be used to perform distributed locks.

sysd-msg-076.title: Distributed monolith: microservices in name only
sysd-msg-076.text: A system can look like microservices and still behave like a monolith. A distributed monolith resembles the microservices architecture but is tightly coupled within itself, like a monolithic application. Signs are a need for low-latency communication, services that do not scale easily, dependencies between services, shared resources such as databases, and tightly coupled systems. Scalability is a primary reason to adopt microservices, yet a distributed monolith makes most components depend on one another, which increases design complexity.

sysd-msg-075.title: Microservices pitfalls
sysd-msg-075.text: Microservices fail to deliver in familiar ways. Service boundaries not drawn around the business domain, a lack of business alignment and a lack of clear ownership are common pitfalls. Teams underestimate how hard it is to build a distributed system, and a lack of design for faults can let failures cascade. A shared database or common dependencies between services undermine their independence, the kind of coupling that marks a {{ref:sysd-msg-076}}. A lack of {{ref:sysd-reliab-071}} and trying to do everything ACID instead of BASE are further pitfalls.

sysd-msg-077.title: Modular monolith: one deployment, independent modules
sysd-msg-077.text: A modular monolith is still one application, built and deployed as a single unit. Its code, though, is broken into independent modules, one for each feature. Reducing each module's dependencies lets a module be enhanced or changed without affecting the others. Done right, this reduces the complexity of maintaining a monolith as the system grows, which pays off in the long term.

sysd-msg-142.title: Strangler fig pattern: replacing old code section by section
sysd-msg-142.text: The strangler fig pattern wraps old code with the intent of redirecting it to newer code, or of logging uses of the old code. In a rewrite, the code is divided into many small sections. Each is wrapped, then swapped out for new code before the next section is tackled. This is less risky and more incremental than swapping out the entire piece of software at once, and it can migrate a monolithic application to a microservices architecture. Logging shows how often old code runs in production, which decides whether to delete it or rewrite it.

sysd-msg-087.title: Incremental migration to microservices: code first, data later
sysd-msg-087.text: Microservices are considered a viable way to modernize an existing monolith, and modernization of legacy applications is done incrementally. The iterative approach migrates application code first, with the new microservices temporarily relying on the existing monolithic database. As the system becomes better understood, the data is decoupled and restructured so each microservice has its own database. That simplifies migration and reduces data migration errors. The trap is the data-driven migration antipattern: prioritizing data migration during the move from a monolith. Replacing code section by section is the idea behind the {{ref:sysd-msg-142}}.

openers.monoliths-microservices-and-service-disc: An application can be one self-contained unit that performs every step of a business function, or a collection of small, loosely coupled services that can be deployed and scaled independently. This chapter walks that range, from the monolith and the layers of an N-tier design to microservices and the older service-oriented architecture. Splitting an application creates new problems. Clients must find service instances whose locations change, a proxy paired with each service can handle their communication, and a distributed trace can track one request through all the services that fulfil it. The chapter also covers how services collaborate, through shared rules for exchanging messages or through a central coordinator.

reviews.monoliths-microservices-and-service-disc: This chapter traces one choice: how tightly to bind the parts of an application. A monolith keeps everything in one unit, N-tier design divides it into layers, and microservices and service-oriented architecture split it into loosely coupled services. Splitting creates new jobs: a registry and a discovery pattern to find instances, a service mesh to handle their communication, and distributed tracing to follow one request across them. Whether to start with a monolith or with microservices depends on team size, business maturity and latency needs, and pitfalls such as the distributed monolith show what happens when the split is done badly. Patterns like the strangler fig and incremental migration describe how to move from one to the other step by step.
